items.title: From FGM survivor to advocate for change
items.description: FGM survivor Rahma Hassan is empowering women and girls to reject harmful practices through community advocacy, counselling and training by Save A Girl, Save A Generation.
content: Female genital mutilation (FGM), child marriage and gender-based violence continue to affect women and girls, limiting their access to education, healthcare and opportunities.
Through counselling, training and community support, survivors are gaining the knowledge and confidence to challenge these practices.

At 24, Rahma Hassan is turning her experiences into advocacy after completing the Kuelekea Mabadiliko training. She now encourages other women and girls to reject harmful practices, seek support and make informed decisions about their lives.

Growing up in a Somali family of seven children, Rahma underwent FGM at six, believing it was a cultural rite of passage into adulthood. She was married at 13 and later experienced sexual and domestic violence.
“Before joining the training, I did not understand FGM beyond what I had been taught in my community. I thought it was just our culture and that every girl had to go through it,” she says.

Her journey towards change began when she met Asha Ismail, founder of Save A Girl, Save A Generation, while working for her. After learning about Rahma’s experiences, Asha referred her to the initiative, where she received counselling, psychosocial support and practical skills training.
Through the six-month training, Rahma learned about the different types of FGM, its consequences, gender-based violence, nutrition and women’s and children’s well-being.
“I can now explain the different types of FGM and gender-based violence. I have gained knowledge that I did not have before, and I am able to share it with other women,” she says.

The sessions helped her regain confidence and speak openly about her experiences without shame or fear of judgement. She has since voluntarily reached out to 30 women survivors, sharing information and encouraging them to seek support.
She has also committed to ensuring her daughters grow up free from FGM.

“I will never take my daughters for FGM. I know what I went through, and I do not want them to experience the same pain. I want them to have the education and opportunities that I did not get,” she says.
“Do not give up on yourself, and do not depend entirely on a man. Even if it is a small job, try to earn something and become independent. You never know which door will open for you,” she says.
The initiative also seeks to build peer networks where women can discuss issues often considered taboo and support one another.

Balkisa Dahir Mohamed, a social worker and Training Manager at Save A Girl, Save A Generation, says participants learn about FGM, gender-based violence, sexual and reproductive health rights, menstrual hygiene, positive parenting and mental health.

“We also look at FGM from different perspectives. We work with doctors, sheikhs, community leaders and other partners to help communities understand that it is not a religious requirement but a harmful cultural practice that needs to stop,” says Balkisa.
Since its launch in 2023, the initiative has trained 340 women. The first cohort comprised seven women, followed by 121 participants in 2024, 106 in 2025 and another 106 in 2026.
Graduates remain connected through a WhatsApp network and support groups, where they share experiences and encourage one another.
“They feel safe because they are among women who have gone through similar experiences. They can speak freely, challenge one another and realise they are not alone,” she says.

One of the groups formed by graduates is Hoora Bulla. Members meet twice a month and save together. The group was registered as a self-help group and received its certificate in June. By November 2026, members had saved KSh153,000 and were exploring business opportunities.
Balkisa says the initiative is also changing how women think about their daughters’ futures.

“They are becoming busy developing themselves rather than thinking about how to cut their daughters. They start asking themselves, how can I empower my girl? How can I take her to school instead of thinking about who will come and cut her so that she can be considered a good girl?”
Beyond Kuelekea Mabadiliko, the organisation runs interventions addressing protection, healthcare and livelihoods.
Jacinta Kahwai, Project Manager at Save A Girl, Save A Generation, says its LINDA umbrella project brings together protection, awareness creation, healthcare training and economic empowerment.
“We exist to fight female genital mutilation, prevent it and protect women who are running away from any form of violence, including FGM,” she says.

Kuelekea Mabadiliko is a six-month awareness course covering FGM, gender-based violence, mental health, women’s rights and female anatomy. Doctors, psychologists, lawyers and religious leaders volunteer their expertise.
Kahwai says some participants initially have limited knowledge of their rights and bodies.

“They come in not knowing much about their rights, their bodies and even the normal appearance of female genitalia. Most of them have already undergone FGM, so they have no idea what is considered normal,” she says.
She adds that graduates are increasingly reporting planned cutting and intervening to protect girls at risk.

“We can see that even as the programme is ongoing, it is successful because we hear cases from women who help prevent FGM. They tell us when someone wants to subject a girl to the practice, and they are able to intervene,” Kahwai says.

Other initiatives include Safe in Nairobi, a shelter for women escaping violence, and Ushonaji wa Ndoto, which equips vulnerable women around Korogocho with tailoring skills and sewing machines. The organisation also runs Mafunzo, which trains healthcare workers to improve their understanding of FGM-related complications and provide respectful care to survivors.
Access to appropriate medical care is another important part of supporting women who have undergone FGM.
Dr Glory Kawira, founder of Vuka Vikwazo Initiative, says her organisation supports survivors of FGM and child marriage through reconstructive surgeries and health education.
Her organisation facilitated sessions on the physical effects of FGM, changes in the female body, reconstructive surgery and available referral pathways.
Kawira said the sessions also helped her understand the concerns women wanted addressed.
“The women here are very open to talk about things that I consider very vulnerable. And that was very useful in us figuring out solutions for them and the education that they needed,” she says.
She emphasised the importance of protecting girls and ensuring survivors know that medical assistance is available.
“The safety of a girl is not an option. It’s mandatory,” she says.
At the county level, coordination between health facilities, government departments and community organisations helps link survivors to services.

Wangechi Muturi, Psychosocial and GBV Services Coordinator at Kamukunji Sub-County, works under the Department of Health, coordinating efforts to prevent and respond to gender-based violence and ensure survivors access integrated services in health facilities.
She also coordinates the GBV Technical Working Group, which brings together government departments, civil society organisations, community-based organisations, young people and healthcare workers.

“We have different stakeholders, including government offices and departments, CSOs, CBOs and young people. We want to ensure that young people are meaningfully involved because they are also affected by these issues,” she says.
The group addresses teenage pregnancies, HIV, FGM, defilement and physical, sexual, emotional and cultural violence.
Speaking during the graduation, Muturi said it was encouraging to see survivors acquire skills that could help them earn an income.

“For me, seeing survivors of FGM coming here to celebrate this milestone is a plus. They have been trained, given information and skills, and are now able to do some income-generating activities on their own,” she says.
She noted that earning an income could help women facing marital challenges provide for their children and reduce dependence on abusive partners.

“Having an income-generating activity would help women stand on their own, whether they have a partner or not. It would also enable them to provide for their children and reduce their dependence on abusive partners,” she says.
Education and vocational training can also open further opportunities for women seeking to improve their livelihoods.
Salome Terah, Director of Adult Education in Nairobi County, urged the graduands to pursue further education and acquire practical skills.

She said the RISE Programme Scholarship offers full sponsorship for tuition and KCSE examination fees to young people aged 15 to 35 in Nairobi, with priority given to persons with disabilities, refugees and women.
“This is not the end. This is the beginning,” she said, encouraging the graduands to take advantage of available learning opportunities.
Terah urged those who had dropped out of secondary school to enrol for the 2027 KCSE examination, which she said would be the final examination under the 8-4-4 system.
“It is your last chance to complete secondary education. Do not let this opportunity pass you by,” she said, adding that online and physical classes were available.
She noted that registration for the Qualifying Test was ongoing at Nyayo House, 10th Floor, Nairobi, for learners seeking to join the RISE Programme and sit for KCSE.
Terah said the Adult Education Curriculum was also under review to create pathways to further education, technical and vocational training, employment and entrepreneurship.
“Learning will no longer stop at literacy. It will lead you somewhere,” she said.

She added that the county was promoting training in tailoring, hairdressing, catering, digital skills and entrepreneurship. Learners completing Basic Literacy and Post-Literacy programmes would also receive certificates to support their progression to the next level.
As the graduates prepare to take their knowledge back to their communities, Kamukunji Member of Parliament Yusuf Hassan Abdi challenged them to become ambassadors in the fight against FGM.
He urged them to share information with families and community members.

“You are now the new ambassadors who will take this message forward and spread awareness in your communities. Let us ensure that this harmful practice is completely eradicated from our country and society,” he said.
Hassan reminded the graduates that FGM is a criminal offence under Kenyan law and warned that those involved could face arrest and prosecution.
He said he began speaking against the practice in 1967, when he was 16, despite resistance from people who believed it was not an issue men should discuss.
“Even my mother reprimanded me, telling me that this was not an issue a man should discuss and that women should be left to make that decision,” he recalled

items.title: Dubai-based businessman charged with defrauding a Nairobi trader Sh172m in gold racket
items.description: It took police eight months to locate and arrest him.
content: Gold bars. Bhadra obtained Sh172.6m from Abdullahi Buthul, pretending that he was in a position to supply him with 210 kg of gold.

A Dubai-based businessman has been charged in a Nairobi Court with defrauding another businessman based in Nairobi of USD1,325,970 (Sh172.6million), claiming he would supply him with 210 kilogrammes of gold.
Maheshbhai Rameshbhai Bhadra denied the offence when he was presented before Senior Principal Magistrate Teresia Nyagena.

Mr Bhadra, who was arrested on November 11, 2026, at the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), Nairobi, after landing from Dubai, has been in prison custody pending determination of whether he will be freed on bond or not.
Ms Nyagena heard from a prosecuting counsel that Mr Bhadra is a flight risk, as it took police eight months to locate and arrest him.

Opposing the grant of bail, the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) Renson Ingonga told the court that the alleged offence is a transnational crime and “there is no guarantee the accused will turn up in court once released on bond.”
The prosecutor urged the magistrate to disregard averments by the defence that the prosecution would liaise with the Indian Embassy in Nairobi in the event the accused fails to turn up for trial.
Also Read: Taxi driver, business woman implicated in Sh54.9 million gold scam

“Although the accused is an Indian national, he is not a diplomat and the charge he is facing is criminal in nature and individualistic. The charge is not against all Indians. It is against an individual,” the prosecutor said.
The court was informed that the accused was apprehended upon arrival from Dubai, then detained as investigations went on.
The magistrate was further informed that the offence was committed in a progressive manner between November 2025 and June 2026.
Ms Nyagena was further asked to consider the plight of the victim who has allegedly lost USD ($) 1,325,970 (KSh172.6) in the fraudulent gold scheme.
The magistrate heard that the prosecution is ready to fast-track the hearing of the case.
The accused, through his lawyer, urged the court to free him on bond, saying “he should benefit from the rights guaranteed to foreigners by the Kenyan Constitution”.
Ms Nyagena was urged not to lose sight of the fact that “any suspect is presumed innocent until proven otherwise”. The court was urged to free the accused on reasonable bond but on stringent terms.
Also Read: Inside Sh5bn fake gold cases, flashy fraudsters and gullible foreigners
Ms Nyagena reserved her ruling on the bail application to November 26 2026.
Mr Bhadra is charged with obtaining through pretences contrary to section 313 of the Penal Code.

The court was told that on diverse dates between November 4, 2025 and June 12, 2026, at an unknown place, with intent to defraud, he obtained USD ($) 1,325,970 (Sh172.6m) from Abdullahi Yussuf Buthul, pretending that he was in a position to supply him with 210 kg of gold, a fact he knew to be false.
He denied the charge and was remanded in prison custody.

items.title: Ranking top in interviews alone won’t guarantee job, court rules in Maseno VC case
items.description: The law did not create an automatic entitlement to recommendation based solely on numerical...
content: Ranking highest in a job interview does not guarantee automatic selection for a public position, according to a Kisumu court.

Ranking highest in a job interview does not guarantee automatic selection for a public position, a Kisumu court has ruled, in a decision that has brought into focus the delicate balance between merit, gender equality and regional representation in public appointments.

In a ruling, Justice Joe Omido dismissed two consolidated petitions challenging the Public Service Commission’s (PSC) decision to forward the names of candidates who finished first, fourth and fifth in the Maseno University Vice-Chancellor interviews, leaving out those who came second and third.

The petitioners, Evans Ochieng Aseto and Solomon Erick Omondi Okello, questioned why Prof Bernard O Aduda and Prof Francis Jakim Mulaa, who emerged second and third respectively, were overlooked in favour of Prof Kimani Chege Gabriel and Prof Mary Jepkemoi Kipsat, who finished fourth and fifth.

The two petitions were consolidated, with Mr Aseto and Mr Okello becoming the first and second petitioners respectively. The Public Service Commission, the Council of Maseno University, the Ministry of Education and the Attorney General were named as the first, second, third and fourth respondents.
Entrance to Maseno University's main campus.
Also Read: Maseno University VC intrigues - Court battle deepens

The petitioners argued that the decision departed from the published interview rankings without any convincing explanation, raising questions about fairness, transparency and the place of merit in public appointments.

However, Justice Omido held that securing a higher interview score does not, on its own, create an automatic right to be recommended for appointment. He said the commission was also required to consider other constitutional values, including gender balance and diversity.

The dispute arose from a recruitment process initiated by the PSC on December 16, 2025, when it advertised the position of Vice-Chancellor at Maseno University, inviting applications from suitably qualified candidates.

The advertisement outlined the academic qualifications, professional experience, leadership skills and administrative credentials expected of applicants seeking to head the public university. Ten candidates were shortlisted, with interviews conducted on April 14 and 16, 2026.
When the results were released, Prof Bulitia Godrick Mathews emerged top with 79 marks, followed by Prof Aduda with 77.5 marks and Prof Mulaa with 77 marks.
Prof Chege came fourth with 76 marks, while Prof Kipsat secured fifth position with 74 marks, tying with Prof Joseph Ouma Rasowo.

Prof Stephen O. Odebero scored 71.5 marks, while Prof Godfrey S. Mise managed 67 marks. Prof Eric Otieno Nyamitha was listed as “Not Ranked”, while Prof Charles O. A. Omwadho declined to attend the interview.
However, when the PSC forwarded its recommendations to the Maseno University Council, the list comprised Prof Mathews, Prof Chege and Prof Kipsat.
The decision effectively shut out Prof Aduda and Prof Mulaa despite their strong performances at the interviews, while opening the door for candidates who had finished behind them.

That became the central point of the legal battle, with the petitioners arguing that the commission could not publish interview scores, rank candidates and subsequently disregard the order without providing a clear explanation.
Prof Francis Jakim Mulaa. He merged third in the Maseno University Vice-Chancellor interviews.
Also Read: Prof Okumu - The physicist who rose through the ranks to lead KU

They maintained that the unexplained selection had turned an otherwise competitive recruitment exercise into an arbitrary process, undermining the constitutional principles of fairness, accountability, transparency and equal treatment.

The petitioners also questioned the treatment of Prof Nyamitha, the substantive Deputy Vice-Chancellor in charge of Academic Affairs and Acting Vice-Chancellor at the time. Despite being shortlisted and interviewed, he was classified as “Not Ranked”, a decision the petitioners considered discriminatory and inconsistent with the principles of fair administrative action.

They argued that the PSC had failed to provide reasons or disclose objective criteria justifying its decision to exclude the second and third-ranked candidates while recommending those who finished fourth and fifth.
The petitioners further contended that the failure to explain the departure from the published order of merit rendered the process arbitrary, discriminatory, irrational and procedurally unfair.
They maintained that, having published the interview scores and rankings, the commission was under an obligation to uphold the principle of merit and explain any departure from the results.

On Prof Nyamitha’s exclusion from the rankings, they argued that the decision was discriminatory and contrary to the principles of fair administrative action, particularly given his position as the substantive Deputy Vice-Chancellor in charge of Academic Affairs and Acting Vice-Chancellor.

Among the reliefs they sought was a declaration that recommending candidates who ranked first, fourth and fifth while excluding those who came second and third, without lawful justification, was unconstitutional, illegal, irrational and procedurally unfair.

They also sought orders quashing the recruitment process and the recommendations made by the PSC, as well as an order of mandamus compelling the commission to commence a fresh recruitment exercise in accordance with the Constitution and applicable laws.
The entrance of the Kisumu Law Courts on June 8, 2026.
Also Read: IEBC staffer with two jobs loses bid to overturn dismissal

Further, they wanted the court to restrain the university council from appointing anyone as Vice-Chancellor through the contested recruitment process. They also sought an order requiring any future recruitment exercise to comply with the Constitution and the law.

The PSC, however, defended its decision, arguing that Prof Chege, who ranked fourth, was recommended on the basis of ethnic balance, while Prof Kipsat, who finished fifth, was selected on gender balance considerations.

Regarding Prof Nyamitha’s classification as “Not Ranked”, the commission said that although he had been interviewed, he did not meet the requirement of having served for at least five years as a Deputy Vice-Chancellor or Principal of a constituent college.

While the petitioners insisted that the selection violated the Constitution, Justice Omido maintained that the law did not create an automatic entitlement to recommendation based solely on numerical interview rankings.

“The Petitioner’s dissatisfaction with the outcome of the recruitment exercise, and particularly with the fact that candidates who obtained higher interview scores were not all forwarded to the University Council, cannot by itself justify the intervention sought. The Constitution does not establish an automatic entitlement to recommendation based solely on numerical interview ranking,” said Mr Omido.

The judge said the evidence demonstrated that the commission had considered candidates’ interview performance alongside other considerations falling within the constitutional values governing public service appointments.

“The Court has found no sufficient basis for setting aside that assessment. The Commission’s consideration of diversity, gender representation and other constitutional values was not a departure from the law; it was part of its duty to apply the law. I therefore find that the petitioner has not established a violation of Article 27 or a breach of any legitimate expectation capable of invalidating the recruitment process,” said Mr Omido.
The court ultimately found that the petitioners had failed to establish sufficient grounds for granting the constitutional and judicial review reliefs they had sought.

items.title: Kenya opposition snubs IEBC and gives commission a December deadline
items.description: Kenya's People's Coalition on Electoral Reforms rejects IEBC talks and gives the commission until December to engage or face public mobilisation from January.
content: The People’s Coalition on Electoral Reforms warns that if the electoral body fails to engage meaningfully before January, it will take its case directly to Kenyans — by all means necessary.

The People’s Coalition on Electoral Reforms rejected the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission’s invitation to talks on Wednesday, with former Chief Justice David Maraga and former National Assembly Speaker Justin Muturi leading a united opposition front that includes former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua, former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro, and several other senior figures.

The coalition was unequivocal about its reasons. “Independence is not a licence for IEBC to operate in isolation or disregard stakeholders, particularly political parties,” Maraga said, accusing the commission of convening meetings designed to validate its existing position rather than address substantive electoral concerns. The leaders condemned what they described as President William Ruto’s interference in the commission’s affairs, insisting he has no standing to speak on its behalf.

At the core of the dispute is Section 39 of the Elections Act — amended so many times, the coalition argues, that Kenya currently has no coherent legal framework for transmitting and announcing presidential results. The opposition is demanding electronic transmission and mandatory public livestreaming of results as non-negotiable preconditions for a credible 2027 poll.
The ultimatum is now formally on the table: engage meaningfully before December, or face the coalition taking its demands directly to Kenyans from January through every democratic avenue available.
The IEBC has been warned. The clock is running.

items.title: UDA-ODM coalition deal: January 31 deadline set for manifesto team
items.description: ODM's Central Committee has given its joint UDA manifesto team until January 31, 2027 to finalise a coalition policy framework ahead of Kenya's August election
content: As ODM’s Central Committee plots a Coast mobilisation blitz and assures members of fair nominations, the party’s potential merger with Ruto’s UDA is moving from political whisper to formal framework.

The Orange Democratic Movement has given its joint manifesto team with the United Democratic Alliance until 31 January 2027 to finalise a report outlining the policy framework that would bind the two parties in a formal political coalition ahead of the August 2027 General Election — a deadline that transforms what many had dismissed as speculative political noise into a structured, time-bound process with real electoral consequences.

The directive was one of four resolutions reached at an ODM Central Committee meeting chaired by party leader Oburu Oginga on Wednesday, as Kenya’s oldest opposition institution accelerated preparations for the most consequential election it has faced since the death of its founder, the late Raila Odinga. The meeting, held against a backdrop of intense national political repositioning, underscored that ODM is no longer merely watching the 2027 race take shape. It is actively deciding which side of it to occupy.

National Assembly Minority Whip Junet Mohamed, speaking at a press briefing after the meeting, was characteristically direct about what the January deadline means. “We want to expedite the process of the UDA-ODM manifesto team,” he said. “We want that process to be concluded latest by January 31, 2027. We want to receive the report on issues that bind us if we were to form a coalition. We’re coming together to advance only Kenyans’ agenda.” The language is careful — “if we were to form a coalition” — but the machinery being assembled suggests the conversation has moved well past the conditional.

The significance of a UDA-ODM coalition cannot be overstated in the context of Kenya’s 2027 political arithmetic. President William Ruto’s UDA controls the government, the presidency and a substantial share of the national assembly. ODM, despite the seismic disruption of Raila’s passing, retains a formidable grassroots network, particularly in Nyanza, the Coast and parts of Nairobi. A formal merger of those two political machines would not merely reshape the 2027 race — it would, in all likelihood, define its outcome before a single vote is cast.

Oburu Oginga, who assumed the ODM leadership following his brother Raila’s death and has moved steadily to consolidate the party’s internal cohesion, assured members that engagements with UDA would continue through established party structures rather than through the kind of informal backroom arrangements that have undermined previous Kenyan coalition agreements. That assurance matters. Kenya has a long and unhappy history of political coalitions formed on personality rather than policy, dissolving under the weight of unmet promises and personal ambition once the electoral arithmetic changes. A manifesto-driven framework — whatever its political motivations — at least creates a basis for accountability.

Internally, ODM faces its own pressures. The Central Committee used Wednesday’s meeting to address growing anxiety within the party about the nominations process, with Junet delivering a pointed warning to members inclined to weaponise the issue. “The party has taken note that people who are not happy with the party should not use the nomination process as a scapegoat,” he said, “because assurances have been given through the Central Committee that nominations will be free and fair.” The warning reflects a reality familiar to any party approaching a general election: the closer the vote, the sharper the internal tensions, and the more attractive the nomination grievance becomes as a vehicle for broader discontent.

ODM Secretary-General Catherine Omanyo sought to project institutional confidence in the face of those pressures. “I want to assure everyone that ODM is the party to watch,” she said. “We are strong and not shaken and used to all manner of waves that come.” It is the kind of statement that parties make when they need to reassure themselves as much as their members — but Omanyo is not wrong that ODM has survived political storms that would have destroyed less resilient institutions.

The Central Committee also announced a grassroots mobilisation tour of the Coast region from 6 to 22 December 2026, covering every constituency and ward in a region that ODM has historically regarded as core territory but which has shown signs of political restlessness in recent electoral cycles. The timing is deliberate. December mobilisation builds organisational muscle before the January manifesto deadline, ensuring that whatever agreement the UDA-ODM team produces lands in a party that is structurally engaged and locally anchored.

What emerges from all of this is a picture of ODM doing something it has not always done well: preparing methodically, managing its internal contradictions with reasonable discipline, and positioning itself for a negotiation it intends to enter from a position of institutional strength rather than desperation.

Whether the January 31 deadline holds, and whether a UDA-ODM coalition ultimately materialises, will depend on factors that no committee resolution can fully control — among them the ambitions of individual leaders, the demands of regional power brokers, and the unpredictable currents of Kenyan public opinion as 2027 draws near.
But the deadline has been set. In Kenyan politics, that is where everything begins.

items.description: Kenya's People's Coalition on Electoral Reforms has given IEBC until December to act on livestreaming, tallying centre abolition and voters' register audit.
content: The People’s Coalition on Electoral Reforms has issued an ultimatum to the IEBC — livestream results, abolish the national tallying centre, and fix the legal framework for counting presidential votes, or face mass protests from January.

Kenya’s opposition has drawn its clearest battle lines yet ahead of the August 2027 General Election, with the People’s Coalition on Electoral Reforms convening in Nairobi on Wednesday to reject an IEBC invitation to talks, present non-negotiable reform demands, and warn the electoral commission that it has until December to engage meaningfully or face direct confrontation with the Kenyan public.

The coalition, co-convened by former Chief Justice David Maraga and former National Assembly Speaker Justin Muturi, brought together a formidable gathering of opposition heavyweights: former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua, former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, businessman and politician Jimmy Wanjigi, Kiharu Member of Parliament Ndindi Nyoro, and several other senior figures. Their collective message was unambiguous and carefully choreographed. The coalition is demanding the abolition of a national presidential tallying centre, an independent audit of the voters’ register, tougher penalties for electoral offences, a decentralised election technology system, and mandatory real-time public livestreaming of results. These, they insist, are irreducible minimums — items on which no compromise is possible.

The timing is not accidental. Kenya is entering the most politically volatile stretch of its pre-election calendar, and the opposition knows it. With nine months separating the country from polling day on 10 August 2027, the window for meaningful legislative and institutional reform is narrowing rapidly. The coalition has set its own deadline: amendments to the Elections Act and regulations must be in place by 30 November 2026, with the IEBC gazetting a decentralised results-management framework by the same date. That is four days from now. The urgency is deliberate.

At the heart of the coalition’s legal argument is Section 39 of the Elections Act, which governs how presidential results are transmitted and announced. Maraga, speaking with the authority of a man who spent years on Kenya’s highest bench, delivered a pointed indictment of the current legal framework. “Listen carefully,” he said, addressing the IEBC directly. “What we are saying is that Section 39 of the Elections Act has been amended so many times and some parts declared unconstitutional that we currently do not have a clear legal framework for handling the presidential election result.” The coalition has drafted proposed amendments that would require results to be streamed every hour, concurrent with their announcement at the polling station, and would establish absolute polling station finality — meaning that what is declared at the constituency level is the final word, with no possibility of manipulation at a centralised tallying point.

On the national tallying centre, Maraga was blunt. “The national tallying centre is a crime scene,” he said. “We will not allow that. And livestreaming must be there.” The reference to a crime scene is not casual rhetoric. It is a deliberate invocation of Kenya’s post-election history — the disputed counts of 2007, 2017 and the contested transmission processes that have left millions of Kenyans permanently suspicious of what happens to their votes between the polling station and the final announcement. Opposition leaders have argued that the national tallying centre has historically been associated with the most contentious moments in Kenya’s electoral process and that its existence creates an institutional vulnerability that must be closed before 2027.

Gachagua raised a separate but related alarm over the expiry of the IEBC’s contract with election technology provider Smartmatic on 24 November 2026 — the day before the coalition’s press conference. The lapse of that contract, he warned, creates an immediate risk to continuous voter registration and raises urgent questions about the commission’s readiness not just for the general election but for the by-elections that must be held in its wake. “The People of Kenya have instructed us that there should be no decision, no discussion that should go on without their involvement. IEBC must know that election is about the people,” Gachagua said. He proposed that the commission engage a technical team led by Maraga to develop a credible shared agenda before any further high-level meeting is convened.

The coalition’s decision to boycott Wednesday’s IEBC engagement was itself a calculated signal. Among those who left the earlier IEBC meeting were Gachagua, Kalonzo Musyoka, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, Siaya Governor James Orengo, Maraga, Muturi and other opposition leaders associated with the reform initiative. The walkout sent a message that the opposition will not participate in a process it regards as designed to give the appearance of consultation without delivering its substance. The coalition was explicit: independence is not a licence for the IEBC to operate in isolation or to disregard the political stakeholders who have a constitutional right to be heard.

The government’s response has been to defend the commission’s autonomy and, according to the coalition, to issue veiled threats against those demanding accountability. The opposition condemned what it described as President William Ruto’s interference, insisting that he has no standing to speak on behalf of an institution that is constitutionally independent of the executive. That accusation — that the presidency is leaning on the IEBC — goes to the core of Kenya’s perennial electoral anxiety: the belief, never fully dispelled, that whoever controls the electoral machinery controls the outcome.

What makes the current moment distinctive is the coalition’s breadth. This is not a single-party grievance or the complaint of one defeated faction. It spans the Democracy for the Citizens Party, the People’s Liberation Party, the Democratic Party, the United Green Movement and multiple civil society and professional bodies. The coalition has drawn in political parties, civil society organisations, faith leaders, professional associations, youth movements and women’s organisations around what it insists is a single unifying demand: that Kenya’s 2027 election be credible, transparent and beyond legal challenge from the moment the first vote is cast.

The coalition’s ultimatum is now public and on the record. IEBC must engage meaningfully by December, or the opposition has signalled it will take its case directly to Kenyans — through mass mobilisation, street pressure and every democratic avenue available — from January. Whether the commission blinks, stalls or engages in good faith will define the entire character of Kenya’s road to August 2027.
The battle for the ballot has already begun. What Kenya is watching now is the battle for the rules.

items.title: Wetang’ula says CCTV showed MP pocketing colleague’s phone
items.description: Wetang’ula says he reviewed the footage with Kimani Ichung’wah and other MPs, but Citizen Digital does not identify the legislator or report any formal sanction.
content: Wetang’ula says he reviewed the footage with Kimani Ichung’wah and other MPs, but Citizen Digital does not identify the legislator or report any formal sanction.

Speaker Moses Wetang’ula says CCTV showed an MP pocketing another legislator’s phone, then denying it when confronted with the footage. He says he urged the member to reflect on the incident rather than describing a formal sanction.

Wetang’ula’s account, reported by Citizen Digital on November 25, 2026 , places the incident during a period of heightened tension in Parliament after a disagreement between members. The Speaker said CCTV footage was brought to his office and that he watched it with Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah and other MPs.

According to Wetang’ula, the footage showed one legislator putting another member’s phone in his pocket. The member was summoned and shown the video, the Speaker said, but denied taking the phone even while seeing himself in the footage. Citizen Digital quotes Wetang’ula saying, “We actually saw a member pocket the phone of another member.”

The report does not identify either legislator, say when the phone was taken, or describe what happened to the device afterwards. It also does not establish whether the member returned it. The account is therefore a public description by the Speaker, not a report identifying the person involved or detailing an independently examined recording.

Wetang’ula said he advised the MP to “wrestle with his conscience for the rest of this term,” adding that some conduct was not expected of members. He used the episode to urge MPs to behave honourably and protect the dignity of the House.

That is the response the report records. It does not say that the Speaker referred the matter to a parliamentary committee, opened a disciplinary process, or announced a penalty. Nor does it report a response from the unnamed MP. Without those details, it is not possible to tell whether the Speaker’s private rebuke was the only action taken or whether any further process followed.

The coverage also leaves the circumstances of the disagreement unclear. Wetang’ula linked the phone incident to a period when tensions were high, but Citizen Digital does not say what the members were arguing about or whether the disagreement involved the people connected to the phone. The account does not explain why the footage was brought to the Speaker, who first reported the phone missing, or whether other witnesses were consulted.

There is no second outlet’s account in the supplied coverage to compare with Citizen Digital’s report. That makes the Speaker’s description the sole account available here; it does not, by itself, show that the incident received little attention beyond the material provided. The central claim in the report is specifically attributed to Wetang’ula, who said he reviewed the CCTV with Ichung’wah and other MPs. The footage itself is not reproduced or independently described in the report.

The remaining questions are practical as well as political: who was involved, whether the phone was recovered, and whether Parliament took any formal action. The story, as reported, establishes what the Speaker says he saw and how he says he addressed the member. It does not answer those questions or confirm what followed.

items.title: EPRA kicks off public engagement on oil production in Turkana
items.description: EPRA kicks off public engagement on oil production in Turkana
content: The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) and stakeholders have met residents of the South Lokichar Basin in Turkana County to sensitise them on the ongoing upstream activities in blocks T6 and T7, South Lokichar Basin.
This follows Parliament’s approval of the project, paving the way for Gulf Energy E&P B.V. to commence drilling in the area, with drilling already under way at the Amosing Oil Field.

EPRA Director General Edward Kinyua emphasised the importance of ensuring that petroleum development delivers national economic and social benefits while safeguarding the interests of host communities:

“As we gear towards the first oil in Lokichar, the Turkana community hosting these resources must be adequately informed, understand the activities taking place and have an opportunity to raise any concerns,” said Kinyua.
According to Kinyua, the discussion are meant to ensure the project is transparent and that stakeholders observe compliance with regulations and standards.
“We want to see petroleum resources developed responsibly, with tangible benefits for the people of Turkana and the country,” he added.
The project’s first phase aims to produce an initial output of 20,000 barrels per day over the next five years, scaling to 50,000 barrels per day in subsequent phases.
The South Lokichar basin holds up to four billion barrels, with the current project focused on the Amosing, Ngamia and Twiga fields.

The project, is expected to generate employment opportunities for locals, nurture new investments in the oil sector, and offer Kenyans a skills transfer window, with Kenyan businesses expected to play a larger role in the petroleum value chain.

Kinyua further said for effective coordination between the national government, the Turkana County Government, the project operator and local institutions was critical in ensuring that these opportunities translate into meaningful and sustainable socio-economic benefits for host communities.

EPRA said it continues to undertake regulatory oversight through technical audits, environmental monitoring and collaboration with relevant government agencies, including the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) and Turkana County Government.
These interventions are aimed at assessing compliance with applicable laws, environmental standards, operational requirements and health and safety obligations.

items.title: Kenya, EU agree on AI, fibre and data adequacy roadmap
items.description: Kenya, EU have concluded their Digital Dialogue in Brussels with a joint communiqué and a roadmap for cooperation on digital infrastructure
content: Kenya and the European Union (EU) have concluded their Digital Dialogue in Brussels with a joint communiqué and a roadmap for cooperation on digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence (AI), data protection, digital public infrastructure and online safety.

The talks took place on 23 and 24 November. They were led on the Kenyan side by Principal Secretary for ICT and the Digital Economy John Tanui and Kenya’s ambassador to the EU, Joash Maangi. The European Commission team was led by deputy directors-general Renate Nikolay of the Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology (DG CONNECT) and Myriam Ferran of the Directorate-General for International Partnerships (DG INTPA).
“The aim is to expand trade, attract investment and create jobs in Kenya,” said Tanui.
Kenya became the first African country to set up a formal Digital Dialogue with the EU in March 2026.

The Team Europe investment pipeline, which combines funding from the EU, its member states and their development finance institutions, includes 3,000km of aerial fibre. It also includes internet connectivity for 3,000 schools, health centres and digital hubs, and Wi-Fi for 400 remote communities.
The two sides are also discussing extending the Blue Raman subsea cable system to Kenya and Tanzania. Blue Raman links Europe and India through the Middle East and is backed by Google.

The EU will put €10 million (about US$11.6 million) behind EU–Kenya partnerships with the European AI Factories, the bloc’s network of AI supercomputing and support centres. The work will start with language diversity and agriculture.
Kenya and the EU are also exploring an open-access AI compute facility in Kenya, where startups, SMEs and researchers could build and export AI solutions.
Technical negotiations on mutual data adequacy are complete. Once adopted, Tanui said, it would be the first arrangement of its kind between the EU and an African country.

Adequacy decisions recognise that each side’s data protection rules offer equivalent protection. That allows personal data to flow across borders without extra safeguards, which could make it easier for European firms to process data in Kenya.

On trade, the European DIGITAL SME Alliance and Digital Transformation Centre Kenya will start a business-to-business matchmaking partnership to boost Kenya’s digital services exports and business process outsourcing (BPO) jobs.

The EU will also share lessons on its Digital Product Passport, which will require many products sold in the bloc to carry digital records of their origin, materials and sustainability. This could help Kenyan exporters meet EU market requirements.
The two sides will also strengthen cooperation on trusted digital identity, including interoperability with the EU Digital Identity Wallet, and on protecting children online.
Tanui said the next step is projects that connect communities, help Kenyan firms win business in Europe, bring in EU investment and create digital jobs for young people.

content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.

Bamburi Cement broke ground on a new clinker production facility in Matuga, Kwale County , in a KSh 32 billion (USD 250 million) investment that will significantly expand Kenya's local cement manufacturing capacity.

President William Ruto officiated the ceremony Tuesday, November 24, alongside Cabinet Secretaries Hassan Joho and Salim Mvurya , Senate Speaker Amason Kingi, Kwale Governor Fatuma Achani, Bamburi Cement Board Chairman Dr John Simba, and Amsons Group Managing Director Edha Nahdi.

Once fully operational, the facility will lift Bamburi's annual clinker output from 1 million to 2.6 million tonnes, while cement production capacity is forecast to grow from 1.8 million to 4 million tonnes per year.

The project is expected to generate more than 10,000 direct and indirect jobs , with employment opportunities spanning logistics, quarrying and equipment maintenance.
Nahdi framed the investment as a long-term commitment by Amsons Group to Kenya's economy and the expansion of local manufacturing.

Dr Simba urged that the surrounding communities must share directly in the project's benefits, citing the Mwachome Village relocation programme as an example. Under that initiative, households displaced by the development have received support including financial literacy training to help them manage resettlement resources.

Governor Achani called for stronger participation by Matuga residents and local businesses in the construction and operational phases of the project, arguing that the community should be at the centre of the economic activity the plant will generate.

Event production firm Wave 360 Africa managed the full groundbreaking ceremony in Matuga, overseeing infrastructure, production, branding, protocol and on-ground logistics.
Managing Director Zedd Mukoya said the investment should open doors for young people in Kwale County.
The Matuga ceremony is the latest in a series of major infrastructure launches presided over by the President in recent months.

On September 30, Ruto broke ground on the KSh 2.2 trillion (USD 16 billion) Dangote East Africa Petroleum Refinery in Lamu, a facility designed to process up to 700,000 barrels of crude oil daily and expected to create more than 60,000 jobs.

IIHF ‘Learn to Play’ Program Lands in Nairobi to Fuel Kenya’s Ice Hockey Dreams
items.description: The International Ice Hockey Federation is hosting a weeklong "Learn to Play" coaching seminar at Nairobi’s Panari ice rink.
content: The International Ice Hockey Federation has brought its weeklong “Learn to Play” coaching seminar to Nairobi’s Panari ice rink, uniting 18 instructors from Europe and Africa to strengthen grassroots hockey in Kenya and accelerate the sport’s growth in non-traditional markets .
READ MORE: Alpha Onyango Strikes Late as Gor Mahia Edge Posta Rangers
Marko Valenčič, an IIHF development and growth instructor for Europe and Africa, said the primary focus of the workshop is equipping coaches rather than directly training players .
“For us, it’s more working with the coaches, teaching them, and then they teach the kids,” Valenčič said .
The IIHF currently has 84 full and associate members worldwide .
While neighboring countries like Tanzania are not yet members, Kenya’s active affiliation and strong working relationship with the global body made Nairobi an ideal host .
Valenčič noted that the program carries a dual objective: preparing visiting participants to replicate the curriculum in their home countries, while raising the profile of ice hockey in Kenya .
Ultimately, the federation hopes the increased visibility will attract more youth to the sport and help the Kenya Ice Hockey Federation secure a full-size, regulation ice rink .
For visiting coaches from traditional hockey regions, Nairobi offers a striking contrast to European facilities .
Toms, a representative from the Latvian Ice Hockey Federation, described the Kenyan capital as a “very special place” and an unusual destination for the sport .
He said the weeklong exchange proves that ice hockey does not require a deep-rooted history to thrive .

“Even in such a country where there’s not a very big tradition for ice hockey, we can still make the game grow and attract new people to the game,” Toms said, adding that he hopes the program sparks a lasting love for hockey in Kenya .

Tamara, a representative from the Serbian Ice Hockey Association who has played for 10 years and helped establish Serbia’s Division 3A women’s national team, admitted she was initially surprised to learn Kenya had an ice hockey scene .
She pointed out the unique logistical hurdles at Panari, including a square rink without rounded corners, unfamiliar equipment cages, and a noticeably small Zamboni .
Despite lacking European infrastructure, Tamara said the local coaches and players impressed her on the ice .
“Even though you have these conditions as you have, I still saw a lot of potential in even the coaches,” she said . “You have to start somewhere, so I think it’s good.”
READ MORE: Liverpool Crush 10-Man Manchester United 4-0 in Pochettino’s Nightmare Debut
For Kenyan coaches on the ground, the IIHF’s hands-on guidance provides a critical blueprint for grassroots growth .
Abdul, a coach at Panari working with the Kenya Ice Hockey Federation, said the program has refined how local instructors communicate with young players and structure their sessions .
“It mainly helps on how well we are talking to the kids, how well we are giving them information, and how to engage them so that they love the game, and to give them a safe environment,” Abdul said .
Looking ahead, Abdul views the initiative as a stepping stone for both himself and the next generation of Kenyan athletes .
H is personal goal is to develop into an international-level coach—and to see local talent reach the sport’s highest stage .
“Seeing Kenyan players get drafted into the NHL,” Abdul said. “That’s my biggest dream.”

items.title: Kenyan, Nigerian, Ugandan startups named as Latitude59 Kenya finalists
items.description: Ten startups from Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have been selected as finalists for the Latitude59 Kenya Pitch Competition, and will now pitch on the main stage at the event in Nairobi on December 4.
content: Ten startups from Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda have been selected as finalists for the Latitude59 Kenya Pitch Competition, and will now pitch on the main stage at the event in Nairobi on December 4.

Disrupt Africa reported last month startup and technology event Latitude59 was returning to Kenya for the fourth year, with startups invited to compete for non-equity funding, partner prizes, and the opportunity to pitch on the main stage.
Ten finalists have now been chosen from a record 509 applications from 25 countries – seven from Kenya, two from Nigeria and one from Uganda.

The Kenyan ventures include Inner Circle, which runs a marketplace where African creators earn money from their audiences through mobile money, paid sessions, subscriptions and direct messages in six markets; Farmsky, which builds AI-powered infrastructure for farmers and agricultural SMEs; Sustainable Africa, which builds data infrastructure designed to make African businesses and value chains verifiable and financeable; and ElementPay, which gives businesses in emerging markets bank accounts in their own names in more than 27 countries.

The other Kenyan startups are MasomoGPT, which helps users learn by drawing on things they already enjoy; Chargebyte, which makes solar-powered charging and Wi-Fi stations to widen access to energy and connectivity; and Bahari Mezani, which provides solar-powered cold storage and logistics to reduce fish spoilage and post-harvest losses along the Kenyan coast.

The Nigerian finalists are Ruralpass, which provides identity verification and risk assessment tools that help banks and insurers serve smallholder farmers, and BetaLife, which connects hospitals, blood banks and donors to improve the delivery of blood and medical supplies.
Uganda’s Kyuka Ventures, the remaining finalist, converts plastic waste into clean LPG cooking fuel.

“What stands out about this year’s TOP10 is the range of founders and ideas,” said Krista Meinarde, head of investor-startup relations at Latitude59. “Put them on one stage, and you get a real picture of where African tech is heading, and these are the teams to watch.”
Before the final, the startups will get pitch training and mentoring from pitch coach Gleb Maltsev.

The winner will receive a “golden ticket” to Tallinn, Estonia. The prize fast-tracks them into the top 30 of the Latitude59 2027 Pitch Competition and covers their return trip. It also gives them the chance to meet investors and potential partners in Estonia’s startup ecosystem.

items.title: Kenya’s AI Opportunity Depends on Building, Not Just Using
items.description: By Timothy Laku Kenya has built a strong reputation as one of Africa's leading technology and innovation hubs. But the next phase of that story will depend on whether we become more
content: Kenya has built a strong reputation as one of Africa’s leading technology and innovation hubs. But the next phase of that story will depend on whether we become more than users of artificial intelligence tools developed elsewhere. We risk becoming highly active consumers of AI without developing enough of the technical capacity to shape it, adapt it and build solutions that respond to our own challenges.

Across Nairobi and other major towns, businesses are already using generative AI to draft content, analyse information, automate customer service and improve productivity. Students and professionals are also adopting AI for research, learning and everyday work. This rapid uptake is important, but adoption alone will not determine whether Kenya captures the full economic value of AI.
The more important question is whether we are developing enough people who can create, test, deploy and govern AI systems.

Using an AI tool and engineering a reliable AI solution require very different capabilities. A bank deploying AI for fraud detection, a hospital using it to support diagnostics, an agribusiness applying it to crop forecasting or a logistics company using it to optimise routes needs more than employees who know how to prompt a chatbot.

These organisations need software engineers, data professionals, machine-learning practitioners, cybersecurity specialists and product teams who can turn AI into working systems. They also need people who understand the sectors in which those systems will operate.

That combination matters in Kenya. A model trained on data from another market may not automatically understand local languages, informal business practices, rural connectivity constraints or the realities of our financial and public-service systems. Technical skills must therefore be matched with local context and domain knowledge.
Kenya’s opportunity is not simply to adopt technologies developed elsewhere, but to build the capacity to adapt them, improve them and develop solutions that respond to our own challenges.
Building AI that works and can be trusted
Developing AI systems is only part of the challenge. We must also be able to establish whether they work as intended.

AI systems can produce inaccurate, biased or unexpected outputs. Organisations need people who can test and evaluate models, identify weaknesses, monitor performance and understand when human judgement must remain in control. These processes should be part of the development and deployment cycle, not an afterthought once a solution is already in use.

Governance will also become a core business capability. As AI becomes embedded in banking, insurance, healthcare, education, marketing and government services, organisations will need stronger processes around privacy, security, accountability and responsible use. Kenya’s Data Protection Act has already made data governance an important consideration for organisations. AI raises the stakes further, particularly as automated systems become involved in decisions that affect people’s lives and livelihoods.
The ability to build AI solutions must therefore go hand in hand with the ability to evaluate their impact and use them responsibly.
Turning local capability into economic value

Kenya already has areas where this capability could create significant value: agricultural productivity, financial inclusion, healthcare access, education, manufacturing, mobility and public-service delivery.

However, locally relevant AI solutions are more likely to succeed when the teams building them understand both the technology and the Kenyan context. This means developing professionals who can identify real problems, work with relevant data, design appropriate solutions and take them through testing and deployment.

It also means recognising that AI capability is not developed through exposure to tools alone. Short introductions to AI have value, but they are not enough to build the depth of expertise organisations need. Professionals require practical learning that includes real data, live projects and exposure to the full cycle, from experimentation and development to testing, deployment and ongoing evaluation.

This is where education and training providers, employers and the wider technology ecosystem have an important role to play. At Moringa, we believe technology training must remain grounded in practical application and the ability to solve real-world problems. As the demand for AI-related capabilities grows, developing talent that can move beyond using tools to building and improving solutions will become increasingly important.
Building for the next phase of Kenya’s AI journey

Kenya does not need to choose between using global AI platforms and building local capability. We need both. Access to global tools can accelerate innovation and productivity, while local expertise enables us to adapt those tools, develop relevant solutions and address the risks that come with their use.

Employers must invest in developing the technical capabilities within their teams and ensure that AI solutions are properly tested and governed before and after deployment. Education and training providers must strengthen practical learning and work more closely with industry to prepare people for the changing demands of the technology sector. Government must continue supporting an environment that encourages responsible innovation, strengthens data protection and creates room for local research and development.
The long-term advantage will belong to organisations and economies that can do more than adopt AI. It will belong to those that can understand it, adapt it and build with it.
Timothy Laku is the Chief Skilling Advisor at Moringa.

items.title: Kenya, EU agree on AI, fibre and data adequacy roadmap
items.description: Kenya, EU have concluded their Digital Dialogue in Brussels with a joint communiqué and a roadmap for cooperation on digital infrastructure
content: Kenya and the European Union (EU) have concluded their Digital Dialogue in Brussels with a joint communiqué and a roadmap for cooperation on digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence (AI), data protection, digital public infrastructure and online safety.

The talks took place on 23 and 24 November. They were led on the Kenyan side by Principal Secretary for ICT and the Digital Economy John Tanui and Kenya’s ambassador to the EU, Joash Maangi. The European Commission team was led by deputy directors-general Renate Nikolay of the Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology (DG CONNECT) and Myriam Ferran of the Directorate-General for International Partnerships (DG INTPA).
“The aim is to expand trade, attract investment and create jobs in Kenya,” said Tanui.
Kenya became the first African country to set up a formal Digital Dialogue with the EU in March 2026.

The Team Europe investment pipeline, which combines funding from the EU, its member states and their development finance institutions, includes 3,000km of aerial fibre. It also includes internet connectivity for 3,000 schools, health centres and digital hubs, and Wi-Fi for 400 remote communities.
The two sides are also discussing extending the Blue Raman subsea cable system to Kenya and Tanzania. Blue Raman links Europe and India through the Middle East and is backed by Google.

The EU will put €10 million (about US$11.6 million) behind EU–Kenya partnerships with the European AI Factories, the bloc’s network of AI supercomputing and support centres. The work will start with language diversity and agriculture.
Kenya and the EU are also exploring an open-access AI compute facility in Kenya, where startups, SMEs and researchers could build and export AI solutions.
Technical negotiations on mutual data adequacy are complete. Once adopted, Tanui said, it would be the first arrangement of its kind between the EU and an African country.

Adequacy decisions recognise that each side’s data protection rules offer equivalent protection. That allows personal data to flow across borders without extra safeguards, which could make it easier for European firms to process data in Kenya.

On trade, the European DIGITAL SME Alliance and Digital Transformation Centre Kenya will start a business-to-business matchmaking partnership to boost Kenya’s digital services exports and business process outsourcing (BPO) jobs.

The EU will also share lessons on its Digital Product Passport, which will require many products sold in the bloc to carry digital records of their origin, materials and sustainability. This could help Kenyan exporters meet EU market requirements.
The two sides will also strengthen cooperation on trusted digital identity, including interoperability with the EU Digital Identity Wallet, and on protecting children online.
Tanui said the next step is projects that connect communities, help Kenyan firms win business in Europe, bring in EU investment and create digital jobs for young people.

content: The Future Isn’t Being Imported. It’s Being Built Here.

For too long, the narrative around African innovation has been about leapfrogging with "lite" versions of Western apps. But Nairobi is no longer just the "Silicon Savannah", it is rapidly evolving into a global testbed for frontier technologies. The era of the simple "Uber for X" is over. The next wave of valuation, the next generation of unicorns, will be driven by Deep Tech: proprietary, hard-to-replicate science and engineering that solves systemic problems at scale.

Startup Grind Nairobi Week will take place from November 23 to 27, 2026, bringing together deep tech founders, investors, engineers and regulators to explore Africa's emerging frontier technology ecosystem.

A massive gap exists in the ecosystem. Deep Tech founders, those building in AI, Blockchain, and Hardware, struggle to communicate their complex value propositions to generalist investors. Meanwhile, regulators are racing to keep pace with the rapid adoption of Crypto and AI, and users are desperate for solutions that actually understand their context.

items.title: Unicef: More than half of Kenya's children are living in poverty
items.description: More than half of Kenya’s children are living in multidimensional poverty.
content: More than half of Kenya’s children are living in multidimensional poverty.

More than half (55.3 per cent) of Kenya’s children are living in multidimensional poverty, as rising public debt, shrinking donor support and delayed government funding threaten to deepen deprivation and reverse years of progress in healthcare, education, nutrition and child protection.

The number of children living in multidimensional poverty increased by 2.7 million from 9.5 million in 2014 to 12.2 million in 2022, even as the country recorded economic growth, exposing the widening gap between economic performance and household wellbeing.

A report, titled The Invisible Toll: Rising Debt, Shrinking Aid and Kenya’s Children , jointly published by the National Treasury, the State Department for Children Services and Unicef Kenya, warns that mounting debt repayment obligations, declining external financing and weak domestic revenue performance are squeezing resources available for essential services.

The findings come as Kenya’s annual debt servicing bill has more than doubled from Sh917.8 billion in the 2021/22 financial year to Sh1.87 trillion in 2025/26, according to the latest Annual Public Debt Management Report.

In the 2026/27 financial year, the government has allocated Sh1.254 trillion to interest payments alone, compared with approximately Sh881 billion in combined allocations to education, health and social protection.
This means that for every shilling allocated to the three sectors, the government has set aside Sh1.42 for interest payments alone.
The study warns that children are particularly vulnerable to fiscal pressures because the services they depend on require predictable and uninterrupted financing.
“Child-critical sectors are particularly exposed because they depend on predictable operational financing and, in some cases, external support that is declining,” the report says.

Between 2014 and 2022, Kenya’s gross domestic product (GDP) per capita increased from $1,451 to $1,748. However, the proportion of children experiencing multidimensional poverty rose from 45 per cent to 55.3 per cent over the same period.
Multidimensional poverty captures overlapping forms of deprivation beyond household income, including inadequate access to education, healthcare, nutrition, water and sanitation.
“These parallel trends do not establish causality, but they show that aggregate growth alone has been insufficient to reduce child deprivation,” the report says.
Children living in rural areas, those with disabilities, orphans and those from households exposed to climate-related shocks are among those particularly vulnerable to deprivation.
The situation has been compounded by declining household purchasing power, with real earnings in both the public and private sectors remaining below pre-pandemic levels in 2024.
Also Read: Don't leave us behind, children tell COP31 delegates

Among the most worrying findings is the deterioration of several maternal and child healthcare indicators between 2021 and 2025, threatening to reverse gains made in reducing child mortality and improving nutrition.

Coverage of the first dose of the DPT/Hexa-Hib vaccine declined from 93 per cent in 2021 to 81 per cent in 2025, while the proportion of births attended by skilled health personnel fell from 79 per cent to 68 per cent.
The proportion of pregnant women attending at least one antenatal care visit declined from 99 per cent to 81 per cent.
Similarly, the proportion of children aged between two and 59 months suffering from pneumonia who received treatment with amoxicillin dispersible tablets declined from 83 per cent to 55 per cent.
Deworming coverage among children aged between 12 and 59 months recorded an even sharper decline, falling from 47 per cent to 19 per cent.
“Routine data signal broad deterioration in maternal and child health services between 2021 and 2025,” the report says.

The study, however, cautions that changes in reporting completeness, population estimates and programme design may have affected the figures, which require further validation by the Ministry of Health.

The decline threatens gains recorded between 2014 and 2022, when under-five mortality fell from 52 to 41 deaths per 1,000 live births, while infant mortality declined from 39 to 32 deaths per 1,000 live births.
During the same period, stunting among children under five declined from 26 per cent to 18 per cent.
The report further reveals persistent financing gaps in vaccination and nutrition programmes.
Vaccine financing requirements increased from Sh4 billion in 2016/17 to Sh7.6 billion in 2023/24, while government expenditure rose from Sh800 million to Sh2.4 billion.
The number of children living in multidimensional poverty increased even as the country recorded economic growth.
Also Read: Washington’s withdrawal from UN agencies tests Nairobi’s global role

The pressure on public resources has been compounded by declining development assistance, with net official development assistance to Kenya falling from nearly $4 billion in 2020 to approximately $2.6 billion in 2023.
External development assistance to the health sector declined from more than $1.1 billion in 2017 to approximately $724 million in 2024, with the reduction largely concentrated in grant financing.

The report notes that several programmes targeting vulnerable children were established or expanded with substantial external financial support, leaving them exposed to disruptions as development partners scale back their funding.

During their early stages, external financing accounted for approximately 77 per cent of funding for the Cash Transfer for Orphans and Vulnerable Children programme, 100 per cent of funding for the Hunger Safety Net Programme during its pilot phase between 2009 and 2012, and 71 per cent of funding for the Home-Grown School Meals Programme.
The government is also increasingly relying on loans rather than grants to finance social protection programmes, creating future repayment obligations.

Since approximately 2018, World Bank lending has provided most of the additional external resources for social protection, while grant financing from traditional development partners has remained largely stagnant or declined.
“Concessional loans can help maintain or expand systems in the short and medium term, but they also create future repayment obligations,” the report says.
Also Read: Will ‘philanthropist’ content creators now ignore children?
Beyond inadequate budgetary allocations, the report identifies delayed disbursement of funds as a major obstacle to the delivery of essential services.
A 2025 public expenditure tracking survey covering nine counties found that 67.4 per cent of sampled frontline service delivery facilities and units experienced delays in receiving operational funds.

Health facilities were the worst affected, with 72.5 per cent reporting funding delays, followed by pre-primary education facilities at 68 per cent, water and sanitation facilities at 62.5 per cent and nutrition service units at 50 per cent.
In some instances, facilities reported waiting more than six months to receive operational funding.

The report warns that such delays undermine the ability of institutions to procure essential supplies, maintain operations and respond to emergencies, even where infrastructure and personnel are available.
“Extended delays undermine facilities’ ability to procure essential inputs, pay for operations, and respond to shocks,” the report says.

Erratic disbursement of funds to county governments has further complicated service delivery, particularly in healthcare, where counties are responsible for primary and community-level services, including immunisation, maternal healthcare and nutrition.
In the 2024/25 financial year, actual monthly disbursements to counties ranged from zero to Sh63.9 billion, despite an approved disbursement schedule.
More than half of Kenya’s children are living in multidimensional poverty.
Also Read: Paradox of denial - The evidence state officials won’t read on child trafficking
The report also raises concerns over the effectiveness of Kenya’s social protection programmes, revealing that only about 11 per cent of children receive a child or family cash benefit.
Delayed cash transfers and the declining purchasing power of existing benefits have weakened the ability of vulnerable households to cope with rising living costs and economic shocks.
The Sh2,000 monthly Inua Jamii cash transfer has lost real value since its introduction, reducing the amount of goods and services beneficiaries can afford.

County officials working in social protection and children’s services reported that planned child protection and child-related support activities had been postponed because operational funding was delayed.

In arid and semi-arid areas, where households are already exposed to drought and economic hardship, officials raised concerns about heightened risks of child labour, child marriage and children ending up on the streets.

“Where families are exposed to drought and household distress, respondents also associated weakened support with a higher risk of street-connectedness, child labour and child marriage,” the report says.
The study cautions that these risks arise from multiple pressures and should not be attributed to delayed funding alone.
It further warns that when social assistance is delayed or inadequate, families may be forced to reduce food consumption or postpone expenditure on healthcare and education.

The report also questions the balance between Kenya’s borrowing priorities and investments in human capital, revealing that external borrowing has predominantly been directed towards infrastructure-related sectors.
Between 2014 and 2022, energy, infrastructure and information and communication technology accounted for an average of 65.7 per cent of external debt allocation.
Health accounted for 3.8 per cent, education 1.9 per cent, while social protection, culture and recreation accounted for just 0.5 per cent.
The report notes that health, education and social protection collectively accounted for less than 10 per cent of external debt allocation under the classification used in the study.
While acknowledging the importance of infrastructure investment, the study calls for a balance between physical infrastructure development and investments in human capital.

“The funding raised through external borrowing has predominantly benefited infrastructure-related sectors while direct allocations to health, education and social protection remain comparatively limited,” the report says.
Tax revenue declined from between 16 and 18 per cent of GDP in the early 2000s to about 14 to 15 per cent in recent years, further constraining the government’s ability to finance essential services.
